sentences.text: Malawania was an extinct basal thunnosaurian ichthyosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now Iraq.
The eyeballs of Malawania were supported by scleral rings made of 13 bones, a structure that helped protect the eyes.
Neural spines at the front of the animal have unique trapezoidal tops, distinguishing them from other forms.
Malawania possesses unusually short, trapezoid-shaped humeri, a feature unique to this genus, with the upper end bearing a unique backwards-pointing capitular process.
The lower ends of these humeri do not broaden significantly and articulate with the radius and ulna.
The foreflippers of Malawania contained four digits, with two originating from each intermedium bone, a specific skeletal arrangement.
The first digit of the flipper would have had more than nine phalanges when complete, with the first bearing a notch.
Malawania is nicknamed the "out-of-time swimmer" because its primitive anatomy contrasts sharply with its Early Cretaceous age.

It is recognized as the first non-ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur known to have survived past the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, approximately 66 million years after the group was previously thought to have gone extinct.
The only known specimen was discovered in 1952 in Iraqi Kurdistan by a team of British petroleum geologists led by Douglas M. Morton.
This specimen was donated to the Natural History Museum, London, in 1959 and catalogued as NHMUK PV R6682.
The specimen was formally described as the new species Malawania anachronus in 2013 by Valentin Fischer and colleagues.
Malawania lived between 132.6 and 121.4 million years ago during the Hauterivian to Barremian stages.

A 2017 study by Lomax and colleagues recovered Malawania as a basal thunnosaur with Ichthyosaurus as the sister taxon of Protoichthyosaurus, whereas in 2025, Lomax and colleagues recovered Malawania within the Ichthyosauridae as part of a clade containing all recognized members of the family.
